section_a.prompt: A sequencing lab analyses a double-stranded DNA fragment cloned from a patient's tumour. Adenine makes up 22% of the bases. What percentage of the bases are cytosine?
section_a.explanation: A pairs with T, so T is also 22% and A + T = 44%. The remaining 56% is G + C, split equally, so C = 28%. 56% is the tempting answer but it is G and C together, not cytosine alone.

section_a.prompt: Part of the template strand of a gene being studied in a protein-engineering lab is 3′-TAC GGA CTT-5′. Which mRNA is transcribed from this section?

options.A: 5′-AUG CCU GAA-3′
options.B: 5′-ATG CCT GAA-3′
options.C: 3′-AUG CCU GAA-5′
options.D: 5′-UAC GGA CUU-3′

section_a.explanation: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template strand, with U in place of T, and is written 5′ to 3′: 5′-AUG CCU GAA-3′. The option with T is DNA, not RNA; the 3′-to-5′ option has the wrong orientation; the UAC option copies the template instead of pairing with it.

section_a.prompt: A therapeutic enzyme made of a single polypeptide chain is treated with a chemical that breaks the disulfide bridges between cysteine R groups in that chain. Which level of protein structure is directly disrupted?

options.A: primary
options.B: secondary
options.C: tertiary
options.D: quaternary

section_a.explanation: Disulfide bridges between R groups in one folded chain hold its overall 3D (tertiary) shape. Primary structure (the peptide bonds and amino acid order) is unchanged. Quaternary structure needs more than one polypeptide, and this enzyme has only one.

section_a.prompt: A biotechnology company produces a monoclonal antibody in cultured mammalian cells. The antibody is released into the culture medium. Which sequence correctly shows the path of the antibody after it is made on ribosomes?

options.A: Golgi apparatus → rough endoplasmic reticulum → transport vesicle → plasma membrane
options.B: smooth endoplasmic reticulum → lysosome → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
options.C: rough endoplasmic reticulum → Golgi apparatus → nucleus → secretory vesicle
options.D: rough endoplasmic reticulum → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane

section_a.explanation: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in transport vesicles to the Golgi for modification and packaging, then moved in secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane and released by exocytosis. The Golgi comes after the rough ER, not before, and proteins for export never go to the nucleus.

section_a.prompt: Liver cells and neurons taken from the same patient have identical genomes but very different proteomes. The best explanation for this is that

options.A: different genes are switched on and expressed in each cell type.
options.B: each cell type has mutated different genes during development.
options.C: neurons have lost the chromosomes that carry liver genes.
options.D: liver cells translate their introns while neurons do not.

section_a.explanation: Body cells share the same DNA; gene regulation decides which genes are transcribed and translated in each cell type, giving each a different proteome. Cells do not lose chromosomes as they specialise, and introns are removed before translation in all cells.

section_a.prompt: An E. coli production strain is grown in a medium rich in the amino acid tryptophan. Which statement describes the control of the trp operon in these cells?

options.A: Tryptophan binds directly to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
options.B: The trp repressor is inactive, so the structural genes are transcribed.
options.C: Tryptophan binds to the trp repressor, which then binds to the operator and stops transcription of the structural genes.
options.D: RNA polymerase binds more strongly to the promoter so more enzymes are made.

section_a.explanation: Tryptophan acts as a corepressor: it binds to and activates the repressor, which can then bind to the operator and block RNA polymerase. Tryptophan does not bind the operator itself, and the repressor is only inactive when tryptophan is scarce.

section_a.prompt: In E. coli, attenuation of the trp operon happens when tryptophan levels are high. Which statement describes attenuation?

options.A: The ribosome stalls at the trp codons in the leader region, so an anti-terminator loop forms and transcription continues.
options.B: The ribosome moves quickly through the leader region, so a terminator loop forms in the mRNA and transcription stops before the structural genes.
options.C: The trp repressor binds to the leader sequence of the mRNA and blocks translation.
options.D: Tryptophan-carrying tRNA binds to the promoter and prevents RNA polymerase attaching.

section_a.explanation: With plenty of tryptophan (and charged trp-tRNA), the ribosome does not stall at the trp codons in the leader, so the leader mRNA folds into a terminator hairpin and RNA polymerase falls off early. The stalling option describes what happens when tryptophan is low.

section_a.prompt: A circular plasmid contains three recognition sites for the restriction enzyme XhoI. How many DNA fragments are produced when the plasmid is completely digested with XhoI?
section_a.explanation: Cutting a circle once gives one linear piece; each extra cut adds one more piece, so three cuts give three fragments. Four fragments would be the answer for a linear DNA molecule with three sites, which is the common trap.

section_a.prompt: During gel electrophoresis of PCR products in a diagnostic lab, DNA fragments move through the agarose gel

options.A: towards the negative electrode, because DNA is positively charged.
options.B: towards the positive electrode, because DNA has negatively charged phosphate groups.
options.C: towards the positive electrode, with larger fragments travelling furthest.
options.D: in either direction, separated according to their base sequence.

section_a.explanation: The phosphate groups in the DNA backbone are negative, so DNA moves towards the positive electrode. Smaller fragments move further, not larger ones, and fragments are separated by size, not sequence.

section_a.prompt: In PCR, the reaction mixture is cooled to about 55 °C during each cycle. What happens at this temperature?

options.A: The hydrogen bonds between the two DNA strands break.
options.B: Taq polymerase adds free nucleotides to build new strands.
options.C: Primers bind to complementary sequences at the ends of the target region on the single strands.
options.D: DNA ligase joins the new fragments into a continuous strand.

section_a.explanation: About 55 °C is the annealing step, when primers bind (anneal) to the single-stranded template. Strands separate at about 95 °C, and Taq polymerase extends at about 72 °C. Ligase is not used in PCR.

section_a.prompt: A forensic virology lab starts a PCR with 5 copies of a viral gene. Assuming the amount of DNA doubles every cycle, how many copies of the gene are present after 10 cycles?
section_a.explanation: Copies = starting copies × 2ⁿ = 5 × 2¹⁰ = 5 × 1024 = 5120. 1024 forgets the 5 starting copies; 50 adds rather than doubles.

section_a.prompt: Bt cotton contains a gene taken from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that codes for a protein toxic to some insect pests. Bt cotton is best described as

options.A: a GMO but not a transgenic organism.
options.B: a transgenic organism but not a GMO.
options.C: neither a GMO nor transgenic, because the gene occurs in nature.
options.D: both a GMO and a transgenic organism.

section_a.explanation: Any organism whose genetic material has been altered by gene technology is a GMO. A transgenic organism is a GMO that contains DNA from a different species. Bt cotton has a bacterial gene, so it is both.

section_a.prompt: A gene-editing team designs a guide RNA that is complementary to a target sequence in a gene, but there is no PAM sequence next to the target anywhere in the genome. What is the most likely result?

options.A: Cas9 cuts both strands of the target sequence as normal.
options.B: Cas9 cuts the genome at random places instead.
options.C: Cas9 does not cut the target, because it must recognise a PAM next to the target sequence.
options.D: Cas9 inserts the guide RNA sequence into the gene.

section_a.explanation: Cas9 only cuts DNA next to a PAM, so without one the target is not cut even though the guide RNA matches. Cas9 does not cut at random, and it does not insert RNA into DNA.

section_a.prompt: After Cas9 cuts a gene, the cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, adding a single extra nucleotide near the start of the coding region. The most likely effect on the protein is

options.A: no change, because the genetic code is degenerate.
options.B: one amino acid is replaced by another, but the protein still works.
options.C: the protein gains one extra amino acid but is otherwise identical.
options.D: a frameshift that changes the codons after the insertion, usually giving a non-functional protein.

section_a.explanation: Adding one nucleotide shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is read differently and a premature stop codon often appears. This is how CRISPR knocks out genes. Degeneracy only protects against some substitutions, and an extra amino acid would need three inserted nucleotides.

section_a.prompt: Which statement best describes the induced-fit model of enzyme action?

options.A: When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape slightly so it fits the substrate more closely.
options.B: The active site is rigid and exactly the same shape as the substrate before binding.
options.C: The substrate changes the enzyme's primary structure so it can bind.
options.D: The enzyme is used up as it changes shape around the substrate.

section_a.explanation: In the induced-fit model the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate as it binds. A rigid, exact match is the older lock-and-key model. The primary structure does not change and enzymes are not used up.

section_a.prompt: A pharmaceutical lab tests a drug candidate on a viral protease. At low substrate concentrations the drug greatly slows the reaction, but at very high substrate concentrations the rate is almost the same as without the drug. The drug is most likely

options.A: a non-competitive inhibitor binding to an allosteric site.
options.B: a competitive inhibitor binding to the active site.
options.C: a denaturing agent that destroys the active site.
options.D: a coenzyme that carries electrons to the enzyme.

section_a.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site, so lots of substrate outcompetes it and the rate recovers. A non-competitive inhibitor changes the active site shape whatever the substrate concentration, so the rate does not recover. A denaturing agent would stop the enzyme at all substrate concentrations.

section_a.prompt: An enzyme assay from human cells is run at 37 °C, then heated to 60 °C. The rate drops to almost zero and does not recover when the mixture is cooled back to 37 °C. The best explanation is that

options.A: the enzyme molecules have been used up in the reaction.
options.B: the substrate has been converted into an inhibitor.
options.C: the heat has lowered the kinetic energy of the molecules.
options.D: bonds holding the tertiary structure have broken, so the active site has changed shape and the substrate can no longer bind.

section_a.explanation: High temperature breaks hydrogen and other bonds, denaturing the enzyme permanently so the active site no longer matches the substrate. Heating raises kinetic energy rather than lowering it, and enzymes are not used up.

section_a.prompt: A plant biotechnology lab is trying to engineer the C4 pathway into rice, a C3 plant. The main expected benefit is

options.A: rice would open its stomata only at night, reducing water loss.
options.B: less photorespiration in hot, dry conditions, because CO₂ would be concentrated around Rubisco in bundle sheath cells.
options.C: Rubisco would no longer be needed for carbon fixation.
options.D: the light-dependent reactions would produce more oxygen.

section_a.explanation: C4 plants first fix CO₂ in mesophyll cells and then release it in bundle sheath cells, keeping CO₂ high around Rubisco so it binds O₂ less often. Opening stomata at night describes CAM plants. C4 plants still use Rubisco in the Calvin cycle.

section_a.prompt: Which statement about glycolysis is correct?

options.A: It occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and requires oxygen.
options.B: It produces a net yield of about 30 ATP per glucose.
options.C: It occurs in the cytosol and produces 2 pyruvate, a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
options.D: It releases carbon dioxide as glucose is split.

section_a.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol, does not need oxygen, and splits glucose into 2 pyruvate with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis; CO₂ is released in the link step and Krebs cycle. About 30 ATP is the total for aerobic respiration.

section_a.prompt: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic cellular respiration?

options.A: It is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, combining with electrons and H⁺ to form water.
options.B: It is split to release electrons for the electron transport chain.
options.C: It combines with carbon from glucose in the Krebs cycle to make CO₂.
options.D: It is the coenzyme that carries hydrogen to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

section_a.explanation: At the end of the electron transport chain, oxygen accepts electrons and combines with H⁺ to form water. The oxygen in CO₂ comes from the organic molecules, not from O₂. Splitting water to release electrons happens in photosynthesis.

section_a.prompt: Human cells grown in a bioreactor run out of oxygen. Which statement describes the respiration in these cells?

options.A: They switch to the Krebs cycle only, which does not need oxygen.
options.B: They convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
options.C: They convert pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
options.D: They stop producing ATP completely.

section_a.explanation: In animal cells, anaerobic respiration turns pyruvate into lactate. This step regenerates NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to keep making 2 ATP per glucose. Ethanol and CO₂ are made by yeast and plants. The Krebs cycle stops without oxygen because NAD⁺ is not regenerated by the electron transport chain.

section_a.prompt: A bioethanol lab investigates the effect of glucose concentration on fermentation by yeast. Flasks containing 1%, 2%, 4% and 8% glucose are kept at 30 °C, and the volume of CO₂ released in 20 minutes is measured. The dependent variable is

options.A: the glucose concentration.
options.B: the temperature of the flasks.
options.C: the type of yeast used.
options.D: the volume of CO₂ released in 20 minutes.

section_a.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured as a result of changing the independent variable, here the volume of CO₂. Glucose concentration is the independent variable, and temperature and yeast type are controlled variables.

section_a.prompt: A neurology research lab studies an infectious agent that causes brain disease in cattle. The agent has no DNA or RNA and is made only of a misfolded protein. This pathogen is

options.A: a prion.
options.B: a virus.
options.C: a bacterium.
options.D: a protozoan.

section_a.explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause other copies of the normal protein to misfold, and they contain no nucleic acid. All viruses contain DNA or RNA, and bacteria and protozoans are cellular.

section_a.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a chemical barrier in the first line of defence in humans?

options.A: Cilia in the airways sweeping mucus towards the throat
options.B: Normal bacteria on the skin competing with pathogens
options.C: Lysozyme in tears breaking down bacterial cell walls
options.D: Neutrophils engulfing bacteria at a wound

section_a.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that digests bacterial cell walls, a chemical barrier. Cilia are a physical barrier, normal skin bacteria are a microbiological barrier, and neutrophils belong to the second line of defence.

section_a.prompt: During a skin infection, mast cells release histamine. The effect of histamine is to

options.A: kill bacteria by punching holes in their membranes.
options.B: make blood vessels widen and become more permeable, so fluid and phagocytes move into the tissue.
options.C: present antigens to helper T cells.
options.D: stimulate B cells to produce antibodies.

section_a.explanation: Histamine causes vasodilation and leaky capillaries, which produce the redness and swelling of inflammation and let phagocytes and complement reach the infected tissue. Membrane attack is done by complement, and antigen presentation is done by antigen-presenting cells.

section_a.prompt: Which of the following is a role of complement proteins?

options.A: Producing antibodies that are specific to one antigen
options.B: Releasing histamine from granules
options.C: Displaying antigen on MHC class II markers
options.D: Coating pathogens so phagocytes engulf them more easily, and forming pores that lyse bacterial cells

section_a.explanation: Complement proteins circulate in the blood and, once activated, coat pathogens (opsonisation), attract phagocytes and form membrane attack complexes that lyse cells. Antibodies are made by plasma cells and histamine is released by mast cells.

section_a.prompt: In an immunotherapy lab, researchers want to activate cells that will directly kill virus-infected body cells. The cells they need to activate are cytotoxic T cells, which recognise

options.A: free antigen dissolved in the blood plasma.
options.B: antibodies attached to mast cells.
options.C: self markers on MHC class II found only on B cells.
options.D: non-self antigen fragments displayed on MHC class I markers of infected cells.

section_a.explanation: All nucleated body cells display MHC class I. When a cell is infected, it displays fragments of the viral proteins on MHC I, and cytotoxic T cells with a matching receptor recognise and destroy it. Free antigen is recognised by B cells and antibodies, not T cells.

section_a.prompt: Which sequence best describes clonal selection and expansion of B cells?

options.A: Any B cell is activated by any antigen, then divides into memory T cells.
options.B: A B cell whose receptors bind the specific antigen is activated, with cytokines from a helper T cell, then divides into many plasma cells and memory B cells.
options.C: Plasma cells divide to form B cells, which then release antibodies.
options.D: A helper T cell releases antibodies that select the matching B cell.

section_a.explanation: Only the B cell whose receptors match the antigen is selected; with help from cytokines released by a matching helper T cell it divides (clonal expansion) and differentiates into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory B cells. Helper T cells release cytokines, not antibodies.

section_a.prompt: A lab engineers a monoclonal antibody to bind a new antigen on a pathogen. To change which antigen the antibody binds, the researchers must alter

options.A: the constant region of the heavy chains.
options.B: the hinge region between the arms.
options.C: the variable regions at the tips of the arms.
options.D: the disulfide bonds joining the heavy chains.

section_a.explanation: The antigen-binding sites are formed by the variable regions of the heavy and light chains at the tips of the Y. Their amino acid sequence decides which antigen fits. The constant region decides the antibody class and how it works with other immune cells, not its specificity.

section_a.prompt: After an infection in the foot, the lymph nodes in the groin become swollen. This is mainly because

options.A: lymph nodes are where antigen-presenting cells meet lymphocytes, and matching lymphocytes are multiplying there.
options.B: lymph nodes produce red blood cells during infection.
options.C: pathogens multiply in lymph nodes because there are no immune cells there.
options.D: lymph nodes store excess blood plasma during infection.

section_a.explanation: Dendritic cells carry antigen through lymph vessels to nearby lymph nodes, where they present it to T and B cells. Clonal expansion of the matching lymphocytes makes the nodes swell. Lymph nodes are full of immune cells and do not make red blood cells.

section_a.prompt: A patient exposed to a new virus is given an infusion of monoclonal antibodies against the virus. This gives the patient

options.A: natural active immunity.
options.B: artificial active immunity.
options.C: natural passive immunity.
options.D: artificial passive immunity.

section_a.explanation: The antibodies were made outside the patient's body (passive) and given by deliberate medical treatment (artificial). The protection is immediate but short-lived because no memory cells are formed. Vaccination would give artificial active immunity.

section_a.prompt: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated people in a community because

options.A: antibodies from vaccinated people pass to unvaccinated people.
options.B: vaccinated people produce memory cells that can be shared through contact.
options.C: when a high proportion of people are immune, the pathogen is unlikely to find susceptible hosts, so chains of transmission are broken.
options.D: the pathogen mutates into a harmless form in vaccinated people.

section_a.explanation: If most people are immune, an infected person is unlikely to pass the pathogen on, so spread stops and people who cannot be vaccinated are less likely to meet it. Antibodies and memory cells are not passed between people by contact.

section_a.prompt: A surveillance lab finds a new influenza strain whose genome contains RNA segments from a bird flu virus and a human flu virus. Both viruses had infected the same pig. This sudden change is called

options.A: antigenic drift.
options.B: antigenic shift.
options.C: a bottleneck effect.
options.D: gene flow between populations of pigs.

section_a.explanation: Antigenic shift is a sudden, major change when two different strains infect the same cell and their genome segments are mixed (reassortment), giving a new subtype to which few people are immune. Antigenic drift is the gradual build-up of small mutations.

section_a.prompt: In CAR T-cell therapy, a patient's own T cells are collected and genetically modified so that they

options.A: express a receptor that recognises an antigen on the patient's cancer cells, and then are returned to the patient to destroy those cells.
options.B: produce antibodies against the cancer cells.
options.C: no longer express MHC class I, so they cannot be attacked.
options.D: release histamine at the tumour to cause inflammation.

section_a.explanation: CAR T cells carry an engineered receptor that binds a specific antigen on the tumour cells; after being multiplied and returned to the patient they find and kill those cells. T cells do not make antibodies; B-derived plasma cells do.

section_a.prompt: A captive colony of a rare frog, kept because its skin makes antimicrobial peptides, is struck by a fungal disease that kills 95% of the frogs at random, regardless of their genes. Several alleles present before the outbreak are now missing. This change is best described as

options.A: natural selection.
options.B: gene flow.
options.C: mutation.
options.D: the bottleneck effect, a form of genetic drift.

section_a.explanation: A sudden, large drop in population size that removes individuals by chance leaves a small, random sample of the original gene pool, so alleles can be lost. This is a bottleneck. It is not natural selection because the frogs died regardless of their genes.

section_a.prompt: A breeding colony of 250 laboratory mice is tested for a gene with alleles A and a. There are 90 AA, 120 Aa and 40 aa mice. What is the frequency of allele a?
section_a.explanation: There are 2 × 250 = 500 copies of the gene. Copies of a = (2 × 40) + 120 = 200. Frequency = 200 ÷ 500 = 0.40. 0.16 is the proportion of aa mice, not the allele frequency, and 0.60 is the frequency of A.

section_a.prompt: Patients with a chronic viral infection are treated with an antiviral drug. After several months, most of the virus particles in each patient are resistant to the drug. The best explanation is that

options.A: the drug caused the virus to develop resistance mutations so it could survive.
options.B: the patients' immune systems produced resistant viruses.
options.C: resistant variants already present by chance survived and replicated, while susceptible variants were destroyed.
options.D: all the virus particles gradually became used to the drug.

section_a.explanation: Mutations arise randomly; the drug does not cause them. The drug is a selection pressure: rare resistant variants survive and multiply, so the resistance allele increases in frequency. Individuals do not 'get used to' a drug in an evolutionary sense.

section_a.prompt: An ancient DNA lab radiocarbon-dates a bone and finds it contains 25% of the carbon-14 it would have had when the animal died. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. The approximate age of the bone is

options.A: 11 460 years.
options.B: 2865 years.
options.C: 5730 years.
options.D: 17 190 years.

section_a.explanation: 100% → 50% is one half-life and 50% → 25% is a second, so the age is 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years. 5730 years would leave 50%, and 17 190 years (three half-lives) would leave 12.5%.

section_a.prompt: A lab compares the amino acid sequence of a respiratory enzyme in humans and three other primates, W, X and Y. The number of amino acid differences from humans is W: 1, X: 12, Y: 20. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: X is the most closely related to humans.
options.B: Y shares the most recent common ancestor with humans.
options.C: All three are equally related to humans.
options.D: W shares the most recent common ancestor with humans.

section_a.explanation: Mutations build up over time after two lineages split, so the fewer the differences, the more recently they shared a common ancestor. W has only 1 difference. Y, with the most differences, is the most distantly related.

section_a.prompt: Which observation provides the strongest support for the 'Out of Africa' model of the origin of modern humans?

options.A: Present-day African populations have the greatest mitochondrial DNA diversity of all human populations.
options.B: Neanderthal fossils are found in Europe.
options.C: Homo erectus fossils are found in Asia.
options.D: Modern humans everywhere have the same blood group.

section_a.explanation: The longer a population has existed, the more mutations it accumulates, so the highest mtDNA diversity in Africa suggests the oldest modern human populations are there and others descend from groups that left Africa. Neanderthal and H. erectus fossils outside Africa do not show where H. sapiens arose.

section_b.stem:
A biotechnology lab produces a human signalling protein, called GF-7 in this question, for use in wound-healing trials. The GF-7 gene is expressed in cultured mammalian cells, and the protein is collected from the culture medium.

The first 15 bases of the coding strand of the GF-7 coding region are:

`5′-ATG TGG AAA GAC TTC-3′`

Part of the genetic code (mRNA codons) is shown below.

| Codon | Amino acid | Codon | Amino acid |
|---|---|---|---|
| AUG | Met (start) | GAU | Asp |
| UGG | Trp | GAC | Asp |
| AAA | Lys | UUC | Phe |
| AAG | Lys | UUU | Phe |
| UGA | stop | UAG | stop |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the enzyme that synthesises pre-mRNA from the GF-7 gene, and state where in the cell this happens.
parts.answer: RNA polymerase, in the nucleus.
marking: 1 mark: RNA polymerase AND nucleus

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the mRNA sequence for this section of the gene, and use the table to give the sequence of amino acids it codes for.
parts.answer:
mRNA: 5′-AUG UGG AAA GAC UUC-3′ (the same as the coding strand with U instead of T).

Amino acids: Met–Trp–Lys–Asp–Phe.
marking: 1 mark: correct mRNA sequence written 5′ to 3′ with U in place of T
1 mark: Met–Trp–Lys–Asp–Phe

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Two variant cell lines are found during quality control. In variant 1, the sixth base of the coding strand is changed from G to A (TGG becomes TGA). In variant 2, the twelfth base is changed from C to T (GAC becomes GAT). Compare the likely effects of these two mutations on the GF-7 protein.
parts.answer:
Variant 1: the mRNA codon UGG (Trp) becomes UGA, a stop codon. This is a nonsense mutation, so translation stops after Met and a very short, non-functional polypeptide is made.

Variant 2: the codon GAC becomes GAU, which still codes for Asp (the code is degenerate). This is a silent mutation, so the protein is unchanged and works normally.
marking: 1 mark: variant 1 creates a stop codon (UGA) so the protein is truncated/non-functional
1 mark: variant 2 still codes for Asp, so it is a silent mutation with no change to the protein

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: GF-7 is a secreted protein. Explain how GF-7 leaves the cell after it has been made by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
parts.answer: The polypeptide enters the rough ER, where it folds and may be modified. It is packaged into a transport vesicle that buds off the rough ER and fuses with the Golgi apparatus. The Golgi further modifies the protein (for example adding carbohydrate groups) and packages it into secretory vesicles. These vesicles move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it and release GF-7 outside the cell by exocytosis.
marking: 1 mark: protein moves from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus in a transport vesicle
1 mark: Golgi modifies/packages the protein into secretory vesicles
1 mark: secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the protein by exocytosis

section_b.stem:
To make a human enzyme in bacteria, a lab builds a recombinant plasmid. The plasmid pVX is 4.2 kb (kilobase pairs) long and circular. It has a gene for ampicillin resistance, a promoter that works in E. coli, and one recognition site each for the restriction enzymes EcoRI and BamHI. The two sites are 1.0 kb apart, just downstream of the promoter.

A 1.5 kb DNA copy of the human enzyme gene is produced with an EcoRI sticky end at one end and a BamHI sticky end at the other. The plasmid is cut with both enzymes, and the cut plasmid DNA and the gene are mixed and joined, then put into E. coli, which are spread on agar containing ampicillin.

Plasmid DNA from two colonies was cut with both EcoRI and BamHI and run on a gel.

| Sample | Bands seen (kb) |
|---|---|
| DNA ladder | 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0 |
| Colony 1 | 3.2 and 1.5 |
| Colony 2 | 3.2 and 1.0 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the gene and the plasmid were cut with the same restriction enzymes.
parts.answer: Cutting both with the same enzymes produces complementary sticky ends, so the ends of the gene can base-pair with the ends of the cut plasmid.
marking: 1 mark: same enzymes give complementary sticky ends that base-pair

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Name the enzyme used to join the gene into the plasmid and state the type of bond it forms.
parts.answer: DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone.
marking: 1 mark: DNA ligase AND phosphodiester bonds

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify which colony contains the recombinant plasmid. Justify your answer using the gel data.
parts.answer: Colony 1. Cutting its plasmid gives a 1.5 kb band, the same size as the inserted human gene, plus the 3.2 kb plasmid backbone (4.2 − 1.0 = 3.2 kb). Colony 2 gives a 1.0 kb band, showing the original 1.0 kb piece was joined back in, so it has the non-recombinant plasmid.
marking: 1 mark: Colony 1
1 mark: justification that the 1.5 kb band matches the gene (with the 3.2 kb backbone), whereas Colony 2's 1.0 kb band is the original piece

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage of cutting with two different restriction enzymes rather than with EcoRI alone.
parts.answer: With two different enzymes the two ends of the cut plasmid are not complementary to each other, so the plasmid cannot easily close back on itself, and the gene can only fit in one way. This means the gene is inserted in the correct orientation relative to the promoter, so its coding strand is transcribed and the correct protein is made.
marking: 1 mark: ends are different/not complementary, so the gene can only be inserted in one orientation (or the plasmid cannot re-join on itself)
1 mark: links this to correct expression from the promoter (or fewer non-recombinant colonies)

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The lab made its 1.5 kb copy of the gene from the enzyme's mRNA using reverse transcriptase, instead of cutting the gene out of human chromosomal DNA. Explain why.
parts.answer: Human genes contain introns, which are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing. Bacteria do not have the machinery to splice out introns, so a chromosomal gene would be translated into a faulty protein. The DNA copy made from mature mRNA (cDNA) contains only exons, so bacteria can translate it into the correct protein.
marking: 1 mark: human genes contain introns that bacteria cannot remove (bacteria cannot splice)
1 mark: the copy made from mRNA has no introns, so the correct protein is made

section_b.stem:
A cancer research lab predicts that the protein made by a gene called *PXL1* helps tumour cells move through tissue. They use CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out *PXL1* in a cultured cancer cell line.

Three groups of cells were set up:

- **Group 1:** untreated cells
- **Group 2:** cells given Cas9 with a 'scrambled' guide RNA that does not match any sequence in the human genome
- **Group 3:** cells given Cas9 with a guide RNA that matches the *PXL1* gene

A scratch was made across a layer of cells in each dish, and the distance the cells moved into the gap in 24 hours was measured. Each group was tested in three dishes.

| Group | Dish 1 (µm) | Dish 2 (µm) | Dish 3 (µm) | Mean (µm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Untreated | 410 | 395 | 425 | 410 |
| 2 Cas9 + scrambled gRNA | 400 | 418 | 397 | 405 |
| 3 Cas9 + *PXL1* gRNA | 120 | 135 | 111 | 122 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the role of the guide RNA in this experiment.
parts.answer: The guide RNA has a sequence complementary to part of the *PXL1* gene, so it base-pairs with that sequence and leads Cas9 to cut the DNA at that exact place.
marking: 1 mark: complementary to the target sequence in PXL1 and directs Cas9 to cut there

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the researchers included Group 2.
parts.answer: Group 2 is a control that has everything Group 3 has except a guide RNA that targets *PXL1*. It shows whether adding Cas9 and a guide RNA, or the delivery method, affects cell movement on its own. Because Group 2 moved about the same distance as Group 1, the large drop in Group 3 can be put down to knocking out *PXL1*, not to the treatment itself.
marking: 1 mark: Group 2 is a control that differs from Group 3 only in the guide RNA target
1 mark: rules out Cas9/gRNA/the delivery procedure as the cause, so the effect can be linked to PXL1 knockout

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean migration distance in Group 3 compared with Group 2. Show your working.
parts.answer:
Decrease = 405 − 122 = 283 µm

Percentage decrease = (283 ÷ 405) × 100 = 69.9% ≈ 70%
marking: 1 mark: correct difference 283 µm used with 405 as the reference value
1 mark: 69.9% (accept 70%)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The researchers concluded that the PXL1 protein is needed for cancer cells to migrate. Suggest one further experiment or test that would strengthen this conclusion, and explain how it would do so.
parts.answer:
Any one of:

- Put a working copy of *PXL1* back into the Group 3 cells (a 'rescue'). If migration returns to about 400 µm, this shows the loss of PXL1 caused the drop, rather than an off-target cut in another gene.
- Sequence the *PXL1* gene and test for the protein (for example with antibody staining) in Group 3 cells. This confirms the gene was actually edited and no PXL1 protein is made.
- Repeat with a second, different guide RNA targeting *PXL1*. If it gives the same result, an off-target effect of one guide is unlikely.
marking: 1 mark: a suitable further test (rescue, confirming the edit/absence of protein, or a second gRNA)
1 mark: explains how it strengthens the link between PXL1 loss and reduced migration (e.g. rules out off-target effects)

section_b.stem:
A drug-discovery lab is studying ProtK, a protease enzyme that a newly found virus needs to copy itself. They are testing a drug candidate, VX-3, as an inhibitor.

Tubes containing the same amount of ProtK were set up with different substrate concentrations, with and without 5 µM VX-3. All tubes were kept at 37 °C and pH 7.4, and the initial rate of reaction was measured once for each tube.

| Substrate concentration (mM) | Rate without VX-3 (µmol min⁻¹) | Rate with 5 µM VX-3 (µmol min⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 4.0 | 1.5 |
| 1.0 | 6.7 | 2.9 |
| 2.0 | 10.0 | 5.0 |
| 5.0 | 14.3 | 9.1 |
| 10.0 | 16.7 | 12.5 |
| 40.0 | 19.0 | 17.4 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.answer: The initial rate of reaction (µmol of product formed per minute).
marking: 1 mark: initial rate of reaction

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify two variables that were controlled, and explain why one of them needed to be controlled.
parts.answer:
Controlled variables: temperature (37 °C), pH (7.4), and the amount/concentration of ProtK (any two).

For example, temperature must be controlled because it affects the kinetic energy of molecules and the shape of the enzyme, so a change in temperature would change the rate and it would not be clear whether a change was caused by the substrate or the inhibitor.
marking: 1 mark: two correct controlled variables
1 mark: explains how one of them would change the rate and so affect the validity of the results

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe the trend in the rate without VX-3 and explain why the rate levels off at high substrate concentrations.
parts.answer: As substrate concentration increases the rate increases, quickly at first and then more slowly, levelling off near 19–20 µmol min⁻¹. At high substrate concentrations almost all the active sites are occupied at any moment (the enzyme is saturated), so adding more substrate cannot speed the reaction up; the amount of enzyme is now the limiting factor.
marking: 1 mark: rate increases with substrate concentration, then levels off (plateaus)
1 mark: active sites are saturated/enzyme concentration becomes limiting

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Use the data to identify the type of inhibitor VX-3 is most likely to be. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: VX-3 is most likely a competitive inhibitor. At low substrate concentration it reduces the rate greatly (1.5 compared with 4.0 µmol min⁻¹ at 0.5 mM), but at 40 mM the rate with VX-3 (17.4) is close to the rate without it (19.0). This suggests VX-3 competes with the substrate for the active site, so at high substrate concentrations the substrate outcompetes it.
marking: 1 mark: competitive inhibitor
1 mark: justification using data that the effect is large at low substrate and small at high substrate, because substrate outcompetes VX-3 for the active site

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Each rate was measured only once. Explain how this limits the conclusions that can be drawn, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: With only one measurement per tube there is no way to check how precise or repeatable the results are, and a single random error (for example a timing or pipetting error) could give a misleading value that cannot be detected. The lab should repeat each condition several times (for example three replicates), calculate the mean, and check how close the repeats are, so random errors are reduced and outliers can be found.
marking: 1 mark: single readings mean precision/repeatability cannot be judged and random errors or outliers cannot be identified
1 mark: repeat each treatment (at least three trials) and use the mean

section_b.stem:
A biotechnology company grows genetically modified single-celled algae in sealed, clear tanks (photobioreactors). The algae make a vaccine protein. To find the best growing conditions, the net rate of oxygen production was measured at different light intensities at two temperatures. CO₂ was supplied in excess.

| Light intensity (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹) | Net O₂ production at 20 °C (mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹) | Net O₂ production at 30 °C (mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | −2.0 | −3.5 |
| 50 | 4.0 | 4.0 |
| 100 | 9.0 | 10.0 |
| 200 | 12.0 | 18.0 |
| 400 | 12.0 | 21.0 |
| 800 | 12.0 | 21.0 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the net O₂ production is negative when the light intensity is 0.
parts.answer: In the dark there is no photosynthesis, but the algae still carry out cellular respiration, which uses O₂, so O₂ is taken up rather than released.
marking: 1 mark: no photosynthesis in the dark but respiration continues and uses O₂

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis at 400 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ and 20 °C. Justify your answer using the data.
parts.answer: Temperature. At 20 °C, increasing light from 200 to 800 does not increase the rate (it stays at 12.0), so light is not limiting; CO₂ is in excess. At 30 °C and the same light intensity, the rate is much higher (21.0), so raising the temperature increases the rate. The enzymes of the light-independent reactions, such as Rubisco, work faster at the higher temperature.
marking: 1 mark: temperature
1 mark: justification that increasing light at 20 °C gives no increase, but raising temperature at the same light increases the rate

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In one tank the CO₂ supply fails. Explain how this would affect glucose production in the light-independent reactions.
parts.answer: Less CO₂ is available for Rubisco to fix onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle, so fewer 3-carbon sugars, and therefore less glucose, are made. In addition, with low CO₂ relative to O₂, Rubisco binds O₂ more often (photorespiration), which wastes energy and releases fixed carbon, lowering glucose production further.
marking: 1 mark: less CO₂ fixed by Rubisco in the Calvin cycle, so less glucose made
1 mark: low CO₂ to O₂ ratio increases photorespiration (or ATP and NADPH are not used and the cycle slows)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The algae also carry out aerobic respiration. Name the part of the algal cell where the Krebs cycle occurs.
parts.answer: The matrix of the mitochondria.
marking: 1 mark: mitochondrial matrix

section_b.topic: Immune response to a bacterial pathogen
section_b.stem:
A hospital microbiology lab is studying an emerging bacterium, called *Bacterium Z* here, that infects surgical wounds. In a mouse model, researchers measured the concentration of antibodies against *Bacterium Z* in the blood after a first exposure on day 0 and a second exposure on day 40.

| Day | 0 | 7 | 14 | 21 | 40 | 44 | 47 | 54 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) | 0 | 10 | 45 | 20 | 5 | 150 | 600 | 450 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: When *Bacterium Z* first enters a wound, neutrophils and macrophages destroy some of the bacteria. Describe how these cells destroy bacteria.
parts.answer: They destroy bacteria by phagocytosis. The phagocyte recognises the bacterium and engulfs it, enclosing it in a vesicle (phagosome). Lysosomes fuse with this vesicle and their digestive enzymes break the bacterium down.
marking: 1 mark: engulfs the bacterium into a vesicle (phagocytosis)
1 mark: lysosome fuses and enzymes digest the bacterium

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a dendritic cell at the wound leads to the activation of B cells that make antibodies against *Bacterium Z*.
parts.answer: The dendritic cell engulfs *Bacterium Z*, breaks it down and displays fragments of its antigens on MHC class II markers. It travels through the lymphatic vessels to a lymph node and presents the antigen to helper T cells; the helper T cell with a matching receptor is activated and multiplies. This activated helper T cell releases cytokines that activate the B cell whose receptors have bound the same antigen, so the B cell undergoes clonal expansion and forms plasma cells that secrete antibodies (and memory B cells).
marking: 1 mark: dendritic cell presents antigen on MHC class II after engulfing the bacterium
1 mark: presents to a matching helper T cell in a lymph node, activating it
1 mark: helper T cell releases cytokines that activate the matching B cell, which clones into plasma cells making antibodies

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use the data to compare the response to the second exposure with the response to the first exposure, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: The second response is faster and much larger: antibody concentration reached 600 units within 7 days of the second exposure, compared with a peak of only 45 units 14 days after the first. This is because memory B cells made during the first response recognise the antigen straight away and quickly divide into many plasma cells.
marking: 1 mark: uses data to show the secondary response is faster and larger (e.g. 600 units by day 47 compared with 45 units at day 14)
1 mark: memory B cells from the first exposure rapidly produce plasma cells

section_b.stem:
Some cancer cells display a protein called PD-L1. When PD-L1 binds to the PD-1 receptor on a cytotoxic T cell, it switches the T cell off. A company has made a monoclonal antibody that binds to PD-1.

In a trial, 120 adults with advanced skin cancer agreed to take part. They were randomly allocated to two groups. Neither the patients nor the doctors assessing them knew which treatment each patient received. Tumour size was measured after 24 weeks.

| Group | Number of patients | Patients whose tumours shrank (%) | Patients with severe immune-related side effects (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anti-PD-1 antibody + standard chemotherapy | 60 | 45 | 15 |
| Placebo (salt solution) + standard chemotherapy | 60 | 20 | 3 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how the anti-PD-1 antibody could help the patient's immune system destroy the cancer cells.
parts.answer: The antibody binds to PD-1 on the cytotoxic T cells, so PD-L1 on the cancer cells cannot bind to it. The 'off' signal is blocked, so the T cells stay active and can recognise the cancer cells' antigens and kill them.
marking: 1 mark: antibody blocks PD-1 so PD-L1 cannot bind
1 mark: T cells are not switched off and so destroy the cancer cells

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why random allocation and keeping both patients and assessors unaware of the treatment (a double-blind design) improve the validity of this trial.
parts.answer: Random allocation makes the two groups similar on average (for example in age and cancer severity), so differences in outcome are more likely due to the antibody. A double-blind design stops patients' expectations (the placebo effect) and assessors' expectations from influencing the results, reducing bias.
marking: 1 mark: random allocation spreads uncontrolled variables evenly between groups
1 mark: double-blind design removes bias from patient and assessor expectations

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of patients in the antibody group whose tumours shrank.
marking: 1 mark: 27 patients

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A newspaper reported: 'This antibody works and should now be given to every cancer patient.' Evaluate this claim, using the trial design and data. In your answer, refer to at least one ethical consideration.
parts.answer:
**Support for the claim:** the trial was randomised, double-blind and controlled with a placebo, and the antibody group had more patients whose tumours shrank (45% compared with 20%, 27 compared with 12 patients). This suggests the antibody does improve the response for this cancer.

**Limits:**

- The trial only tested adults with advanced skin cancer. Other cancers may not display PD-L1, so the results cannot be generalised to every cancer patient.
- The sample was small (60 per group) and only followed patients for 24 weeks; larger, longer trials are needed to know whether patients live longer and whether the results are reproducible.
- Severe immune-related side effects were five times as common (15% compared with 3%), probably because active T cells also attack healthy self tissue.

**Ethics:** under the principle of non-maleficence, the harm from side effects must be weighed against the benefit, and giving it to all patients without evidence for their cancer could cause harm with no benefit. Patients must give informed consent knowing these risks (respect for persons), and justice means access should be fair once it is shown to work.

**Conclusion:** the claim is not fully supported. The antibody appears effective for advanced skin cancer, but it should not be given to every cancer patient until it is tested in other cancers and its risks are better understood.
marking: 1 mark: identifies evidence supporting the claim (randomised, double-blind, controlled; 45% vs 20% response)
1 mark: identifies a limitation in generalising the results (only one cancer type/adults, small sample, short time)
1 mark: discusses side effects as a risk with an explanation (e.g. T cells attacking healthy tissue)
1 mark: relevant ethical consideration (e.g. non-maleficence, informed consent, justice) and a reasoned overall judgement

section_b.stem: A new respiratory virus, called Virus K in this question, has been found in people in a farming district. The virus normally lives in bats and appears to have passed to farm animals and then to the farm workers. Cases have increased quickly over three months and have now been reported in two other countries. A public health lab is developing an mRNA vaccine that codes for the virus's surface spike protein.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the disease caused by Virus K is described as an emerging disease.
parts.answer: It is a disease that has newly appeared in the human population and is rapidly increasing in incidence and geographic range (it has spread to other countries).
marking: 1 mark: new to the population AND increasing in incidence or geographic range

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the mRNA vaccine would give a person long-term protection against Virus K.
parts.answer: The mRNA enters some of the person's cells, where ribosomes translate it into the spike protein (the mRNA does not enter the nucleus and is soon broken down). The spike protein acts as a non-self antigen: it is taken up and presented by antigen-presenting cells, activating matching helper T cells, B cells and cytotoxic T cells by clonal selection. Plasma cells make antibodies and, importantly, memory B and T cells are formed. If the person later meets Virus K, memory cells produce a fast, strong secondary response that destroys the virus before disease develops.
marking: 1 mark: cells translate the mRNA into the spike protein, which acts as an antigen
1 mark: antigen is presented and triggers an adaptive response with clonal selection of matching lymphocytes
1 mark: memory cells form, giving a fast, strong secondary response on later infection

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe two strategies, other than vaccination, that health authorities could use to slow the spread of Virus K.
parts.answer:
Any two, for example:

- Contact tracing and quarantine/isolation of infected people and their close contacts, so they cannot pass the virus on.
- Testing and culling or isolating infected farm animals, to remove the animal source of infection.
- Travel restrictions or screening at borders, to reduce spread between regions.
- Mask wearing, hand washing and physical distancing, which reduce transmission of respiratory droplets.
marking: 1 mark: first suitable strategy with how it reduces transmission
1 mark: second suitable strategy with how it reduces transmission

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The lab expects that the vaccine may need to be updated in future years. Explain why.
parts.answer: Mutations in the spike protein gene build up over time (antigenic drift), changing the shape of the antigen, so antibodies and memory cells made against the old spike may no longer bind to it.
marking: 1 mark: mutations change the spike antigen (antigenic drift) so existing antibodies/memory cells no longer recognise it

section_b.stem:
A lab studying antibiotic resistance grew one population of *E. coli* in a flask, transferring a sample to fresh medium each day. The antibiotic ciprofloxacin was added from day 5, and its concentration was doubled every 5 days after that. A control population was grown the same way but with no antibiotic. The frequency of an allele of the *gyrA* gene that gives ciprofloxacin resistance (*gyrA-R*) was measured.

| Day | Ciprofloxacin in test flask (µg mL⁻¹) | Frequency of *gyrA-R*, test flask | Frequency of *gyrA-R*, control flask |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0.002 | 0.002 |
| 5 | 0.05 | 0.04 | 0.001 |
| 10 | 0.1 | 0.35 | 0.003 |
| 15 | 0.2 | 0.88 | 0.002 |
| 20 | 0.4 | 0.99 | 0.002 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the change in the frequency of *gyrA-R* in the test flask in terms of natural selection.
parts.answer: At the start there was variation: a few bacteria (0.2%) already carried the *gyrA-R* allele, which had arisen by random mutation. Ciprofloxacin acted as a selection pressure, killing or stopping the growth of bacteria without the allele. Bacteria with *gyrA-R* survived and reproduced, passing the allele to their offspring, so its frequency rose each generation, from 0.002 to 0.99 by day 20.
marking: 1 mark: variation existed before the antibiotic, with the allele arising by random mutation
1 mark: ciprofloxacin is a selection pressure that kills susceptible bacteria
1 mark: resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the allele so its frequency increases (with data)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the control flask shows.
parts.answer: In the control flask the frequency stayed at about 0.002, showing that without the antibiotic the allele does not increase. So the rise in the test flask was caused by selection by ciprofloxacin and not by mutation or chance alone.
marking: 1 mark: without antibiotic the frequency stays low, so the increase was caused by the antibiotic

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Resistance alleles can also pass from one species of bacteria to another. Name and describe this process.
parts.answer: Horizontal (lateral) gene transfer. A bacterium can pass a copy of a plasmid carrying a resistance gene to another bacterium, even of a different species, through a connecting tube (conjugation), so the receiving bacterium becomes resistant without reproduction taking place.
marking: 1 mark: horizontal gene transfer (accept conjugation)
1 mark: description, e.g. plasmid carrying the resistance gene passed directly between bacteria

section_b.stem:
To trace the source of Virus K (from Question 8), a genomics lab sequenced the same 1500-base gene from five virus samples: two from bats (Bat-1 and Bat-2), one from a farm animal, and two from patients (Human-A and Human-B). The number of base differences between each pair of samples is shown.

| | Bat-1 | Bat-2 | Farm animal | Human-A | Human-B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bat-1** | – | 30 | 31 | 32 | 32 |
| **Bat-2** | | – | 18 | 19 | 19 |
| **Farm animal** | | | – | 6 | 6 |
| **Human-A** | | | | – | 2 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the non-human sample most closely related to the human samples. Explain how the data support the idea that the virus reached humans through farm animals.
parts.answer: The farm animal sample. It differs from both human samples by only 6 bases, far fewer than the bat samples (19 and 32), so it shares the most recent common ancestor with the human viruses. This suggests the human virus came from the farm animal virus, which itself came from bats (Bat-2 is the closest bat virus).
marking: 1 mark: farm animal sample
1 mark: uses data (6 differences compared with 19 or more for the bats) to show the most recent common ancestor is shared with the farm animal virus

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Assume that differences between two virus lineages build up at a constant rate of 4 base differences per year. Estimate how long ago the farm animal and human viruses shared a common ancestor, and state one limitation of this estimate.
parts.answer:
Time = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 years.

Limitation: mutation rates may not be constant over time or between hosts, and later mutations can occur at a site that has already changed (hiding earlier changes), so the molecular clock gives only an estimate.
marking: 1 mark: 1.5 years
1 mark: valid limitation (e.g. mutation rate may not be constant; repeated mutations at the same site)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify which sample is the outgroup (the most distantly related) in a phylogenetic tree of these five samples.
parts.answer: Bat-1, because it has the most differences (30–32) from all the other samples.
marking: 1 mark: Bat-1

section_b.stem: A medical entomology lab studies two populations of mosquitoes that carry a human disease. One population lives on the wet coastal side of a mountain range and the other on the dry inland side. Fossil and DNA evidence suggest they came from a single ancestral population about 2 million years ago, when the mountains formed. In the lab, males and females from the two populations mate, but the male hybrid offspring are always sterile.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how allopatric speciation could have produced the two populations.
parts.answer: When the mountain range formed it became a geographical barrier, splitting the ancestral population in two and stopping gene flow between them. Each side had different environments (wet and dry) and so different selection pressures; along with different mutations and genetic drift, this changed the allele frequencies of the two gene pools in different ways. Over a long time the gene pools became so different that the populations became reproductively isolated, so they can no longer produce fertile offspring together.
marking: 1 mark: geographical barrier separates the populations and stops gene flow
1 mark: different selection pressures (and/or mutation, drift) change allele frequencies differently in each population
1 mark: over time this leads to reproductive isolation, forming separate species

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the lab results support the conclusion that the two populations are now separate species.
parts.answer: Under the biological species concept, members of a species produce viable and fertile offspring. The hybrid males are sterile, so the populations are reproductively isolated (post-zygotic isolation) and are separate species.
marking: 1 mark: hybrids are not fertile, showing reproductive isolation, so they are not the same species

section_b.stem: A palaeogenomics lab extracted DNA from a fossil tooth found in a cave in Asia. The DNA showed that the tooth belonged to a Denisovan, an extinct group of the genus *Homo*. The tooth was in a sediment layer just below a layer of volcanic ash that was dated as 80 000 years old using radiometric dating. Other studies have found that the genomes of present-day people from Papua New Guinea contain a few per cent Denisovan DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain what the presence of Denisovan DNA in present-day Papua New Guinean people tells us about the history of *Homo sapiens*.
parts.answer: It shows that *Homo sapiens*, after leaving Africa, interbred with Denisovans in Asia. The offspring of these matings were fertile, so Denisovan DNA was passed down through the generations and is still found in the descendants of those populations today.
marking: 1 mark: Homo sapiens interbred with Denisovans (after migrating out of Africa)
1 mark: hybrid offspring were fertile, so Denisovan DNA was passed to present-day descendants

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State what can be concluded about the age of the tooth, and the principle used.
parts.answer: The tooth is older than 80 000 years, because by the law of superposition lower layers of sediment were laid down before the layers above them.
marking: 1 mark: older than 80 000 years AND law of superposition (lower layers are older)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Ancient DNA is rarely recovered from fossils found in hot, wet tropical regions. Suggest why.
parts.answer: DNA breaks down over time after death, and heat and moisture speed up this breakdown (and the growth of microorganisms), so little intact DNA survives.
marking: 1 mark: heat and moisture speed up DNA degradation
